title: The last disciple
hook: the wanderer Subhadda is turned away at the door; the Buddha calls him in (DN 16)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kusinara. The Buddha lay down, awake, and the trees bloomed. Your line: rest is part of the path.

Arriving just as the doors close. The store's locking up. Visiting hours ended five minutes ago. Someone behind the glass shakes their head: sorry, too late. In Kusinara that night, word goes around: the teacher Gotama will pass away in the last watch of the night. A wandering seeker named Subhadda hears it. He's not a follower; he belongs to another group of wanderers. But a question has been nagging at him for years, and he thinks this teacher might be the one who can clear it up. Now or never. So he hurries out to the sal grove, in the dark.
screen: `JUST AS THE DOORS CLOSE.` → `A WANDERER WITH A QUESTION.` → `NOW OR NEVER.`

segments.voice: At the edge of the grove, Subhadda meets Ananda and asks: may I see the teacher? Ananda, loyal, exhausted, grieving, says: enough, friend Subhadda. Don't trouble him. He's weary. Subhadda asks again. No. A third time. No. You can understand Ananda completely; he's protecting someone he loves in his last hours. But the Buddha, lying between the trees, hears them. Enough, Ananda, he says. Don't keep Subhadda out. Let him come. Whatever he asks, he'll ask because he wants to understand, not to bother me. So Subhadda comes in, sits, and asks. All these famous teachers, heads of big schools, each says he's found the truth. Have they all really understood? Or none of them? Or some? The Buddha waves the comparison away. Let that be, Subhadda. Never mind them. I'll teach you the thing itself. Wherever the noble eightfold path is found, there you'll find people who truly practice it and reach its fruits. Subhadda asks to go forth, right there, and the Buddha asks Ananda to ordain him. The text says that, living earnestly, not long after, Subhadda reached the goal. He was the last person the Buddha taught directly. Notice who got in. Not a longtime monk. An outsider from another group, arriving after hours with a question. And the dying teacher overrode his own protective attendant to make room. The door wasn't closed yet.
screen: `ENOUGH, DON'T TROUBLE HIM.` · `LET HIM COME.` · `NEVER MIND THE OTHERS.` · `THE LAST ONE HE TAUGHT.` · then, large: `THERE'S STILL TIME.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who shows up late in your life: the friend who always texts after the plans are set, the person who joined the team last, or a question you keep putting off because it came at a bad time. Picture the door, your hand on it, about to close. Then open it a little wider; there's room.
Subhadda. The wanderer turned away three times at the door, and called in by the dying Buddha himself, the last disciple he taught.
Your line: there's still time. Turned away three times, and still he got in. Eighty-three days, and counting.

howItsDone: Buddhists remember Subhadda as the last disciple the Buddha personally taught, and the story is often told to show that the door to the teaching stays open to anyone who asks sincerely.

fork.setup: you're dying, and you hear your attendant turning away a stranger with a sincere question. what do you do?
options: send a short message and rest.
fork.reveal: he says: enough, Ananda. let him come. Subhadda becomes the last person the Buddha taught directly.

original.note: Pali: a name meaning auspicious, fortunate. Su (good) and bhadda (blessed).

trapdoor: what you thought: a latecomer who got lucky.
what it means: an outsider turned away three times, and a dying teacher who made room for him.
what a scholar hears: DN 16, 5.23–5.30: Subhadda the paribbajaka; the Buddha sets aside the question about six rival teachers and points to the eightfold path; the last personally ordained disciple.
recall: birth; here, his new life as a monk

notes: The Buddha's answer is summarized: in DN 16 he says that where the eightfold path is found, the first, second, third and fourth kinds of samana (stages of awakening) are found. The script paraphrases this without naming or judging the other teachers. Confirm it stays within 'never rank traditions'.
The usual four-month probation for former members of other sects is waived or shortened in the text; omitted. Confirm.
